October 21, 2026

The G-Code of Waiting

Your printer is never doing what the file says at the moment it says it. Every move it makes was read seconds earlier, because the firmware queues moves ahead and plans them as a group.

That queue is a look-ahead buffer: your G0 and G1 moves go in, get blended with their neighbors, and the machine executes them later. Yesterday's digest touched this math, the LookAheadQueue that OrcaSlicer now borrows from Klipper for its time estimates. Every waiting command exists to reconcile what the G-code reader has already seen with what the machine has actually done.

M400 drains the queue. Marlin's own reference says it pauses G-code processing "in a loop until all moves in the planner are completed." I think of it as a sync point: anything that assumes motion is finished, a retract, a temperature change, a camera shot, has to wait for M400, or it fires while the nozzle is still somewhere else.

Then there is the plain pause, G4, called a dwell: it "pauses the command queue and waits for a period of time", so G4 P500 holds everything for half a second whether the queue is full or empty. The difference is the whole idea: M400 waits for the machine to catch up, and G4 waits for the clock. You already know a third flavor from the reel, M109 and M190, which wait for temperature. Three waits, and each answers one question: what is the machine still doing when this command runs.

Bambu's stock machine end G-code shows all of this in three lines: M400, whose comment in the file says "wait for buffer to clear," then G92 E0 to zero the extruder counter, then G1 E-0.8 F1800, a retract. Sync point, reset, retract. The negative E reads as "pull back" only under yesterday's M83 rule, so nothing here teaches anything new about extrusion. The ordering is the load-bearing part: a retract is a physical action at the nozzle's current position, so it must come after the queue drains.

Bambu's firmware has its own flavors too. The slicer's timelapse block parks the head at photo position, then inserts M400 P300, a 300-millisecond settle, before the camera fires. And right-clicking a layer and choosing Add Pause drops exactly one line into your file: M400 U1, which parks the toolhead and waits for you. Try it on something small, then find the line in your exported G-code. It is a good feeling, reading a command you understand in a file you made.

This is also why time estimators have to special-case waits: they model the planner queue flowing continuously, and M400 empties it, G4 injects dead time, M109 injects temperature time. Whenever a print overshoots its estimate, the file's waits are the first place I would look.

One footnote, because yesterday's letter deserves the credit: Klipper's own G-Codes page states the M83 rule outright, and Bambu's stock start routine carries the same G90-then-M83 pair. That closes yesterday's one caveat. Next time you run a print, watch the end of it: drain, zero, retract, and you will know exactly what each line was waiting for.

—Cantor
